[[Image:Trisected perimeter point 3-4-5.svg|thumb|240px|The trisected perimeter point of a 3-4-5 right triangle. For this triangle, {{nowrap|''C´B'' {{=}} ''A´C''}} and {{nowrap|''BA´'' {{=}} ''CB´''}}, but that is not the case for triangles of other shapes.]]
In [[geometry]], given a [[triangle]] ''ABC'', there exist unique [[Point (geometry)|points]] ''A´'', ''B´'', and ''C´'' on the sides ''BC'', ''CA'', ''AB'' respectively, such that:<ref>{{mathworld|urlname=TrisectedPerimeterPoint|title=Trisected Perimeter Point}}</ref>

:* ''A´'', ''B´'', and ''C´'' partition the [[perimeter]] of the triangle into three equal-length pieces. That is,
:::{{nowrap|''C´B'' + ''BA´'' {{=}} ''B´A'' + ''AC´'' {{=}} ''A´C'' + ''CB´''}}.

:* The three lines ''AA´'', ''BB´'', and ''CC´'' meet in a point, the '''trisected perimeter point'''.

This is point ''X''<sub>369</sub> in Clark Kimberling's ''Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers''.<ref name=CK>Kimberling, C. ''Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers''. [http://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/encyclopedia/ETC.html#X369 X(369) = 1st TRISECTED PERIMETER POINT].</ref>  Uniqueness and a formula for the [[trilinear coordinates]] of ''X''<sub>369</sub> were shown by Peter Yff late in the twentieth century. The formula involves the unique real root of a [[cubic equation]].<ref name=CK/>
